text:
The archives were a mausoleum now, the hum no longer a groan but a deep, resonant thrum in the air itself, the kind that made your eardrums ache. David’s phone was dead weight in his hand, a black mirror reflecting the faint glow of his own anxious face. The impossible timestamp he’d scrawled in his notebook—'07:63:7.56'—felt less like a typo and more like a wound, a number torn from the fabric of time. He stared at the name he’d found: L. Huang. A consultant, Thorne’s silent partner in dismantling Blackwood Bay, a ghost word made solid. But the silence that followed, after the microfilm reader sputtered and died, was total, a vacuum pulling at his thoughts. The digital maw hadn't just eaten the signal; it had consumed the very idea of transmission, leaving behind only the echo of his own accelerated heartbeat.

He reached into his pocket, his fingers closing around the crumpled manuscript page, the one that had detailed the Peterson cabin. Its paper felt impossibly cold, as if it had been stored at the bottom of the bay. The words written on it were his own, yet he swore he hadn't penned them. The creeping thought returned, unbidden, that *he* was the conduit, the mechanism by which the unseen forces in Blackwood Bay were making their demands known. L. Huang, Thorne, Iris, the silent lighthouse – all threads being woven into a story he was only just beginning to read, a story whose ending felt increasingly inevitable, and increasingly dark. The faint, phosphorescent glow from a patch of damp on the wall, near the forgotten portrait, pulsed faintly, like a sick heart.
